quotes.text: The word feasible matters more than fast. A schedule can look neat and still fail the moment production tries to follow it.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Defines the real quality criterion for a production schedule.

quotes.text: The issue isn't whether people use Excel. It's whether Excel and experience can still keep pace with change.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Reframes the software buying question around variation instead of tools.

quotes.text: A better question is, if we expedite this, what will it delay? And are we willing to accept that result? The first asks for effort, the second asks for a decision.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Turns expediting from a reflex into an owned trade-off.

quotes.text: A plan that can't explain itself becomes another source of arguments rather than a tool for good decisions.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: States why explainability decides whether planners trust a schedule.

quotes.text: Fabric doesn't generate a feasible schedule. It stores data, transforms it, governs access and supports analytics. It connects the dots between IT and OT.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Draws a clear architectural boundary between the data platform and the planning engine.

takeaways: Production planning software becomes necessary when changes, shared resources and dependencies outpace what planners can test manually, not when the company reaches a certain size.
ERP owns demand and materials and MES records execution, while a planning layer must test feasible sequences against real capacity, setup, material and qualification constraints.

Start with one failing decision, a clear process and trusted product, process and resource data, run the new plan in parallel, and use Fabric, Power BI and Power Platform around the engine, not instead of it.
hook: Many factories run on a planner who stitches together ERP dates, spreadsheets, whiteboards and phone calls until the plan breaks. This episode helps manufacturing and operations leaders recognize the warning signs that manual planning has hit its limit and shows how to introduce planning software that produces feasible, explainable schedules.
